tone_statements.citation: Badenoch, Nathan. 2022. Speaking Like a Ghost: Registers of Intimacy and Incompatibility in the Forests of Northern Laos. Journal of the Siam Society 110(1): 103-150.
tone_statements.quote: Another interesting feature that remains to be explained in terms of the history of the language is the existence of a two-way tone contrast on many word pairs in Ksingmul – a mid- to low-pitch tone that is more prominent, and a high-rising-pitch tone that is more marked. Contrasting pairs include: hreɲ ‘intestine’ and hréɲ ‘bamboo grub’, tal ‘downstream’ and tál ‘to touch, to disturb’, kaw ‘raw’ and káw ‘unpounded rice’ and ruu ‘to burn’ and rúu ‘to hurry’. Some borrowed Tai words have a high rising pitch, providing lexical contrast with a native word
tone_statements.locator: p. 113, language-background part of the article before 'Register as social history'; continued p. 115 with fn. 5-6 (p. 113); see also p. 107 on múul 'hill'

sources.note: Nothing on Ksingmul stress (the word 'stress' does not occur). p. 139 gives the general Mon-Khmer template 'weak-syllable (with reduction of vocalic and prosodic features) + strong-syllable (with maximum vowel and prosody differences)' (sesquisyllabic); p. 144 says Ksingmul is 'more preservative' and Ksingmul Nghệt 'retains the most sesquisyllabic structures'; p. 146 clusters arise when 'the vowel of weak first syllable, usually [ə] is syncopied'; Ksingmul initials of the main syllable cited from Pram et al. 1990:17; Kháng has six tones (p. 150). archived copy (Internet Archive, 31 Jul 2024)…

sources.note: States first-hand that Ksingmul (Laos, Nget) has a two-way tone contrast on many word pairs: an unmarked, more frequent mid-to-low pitch versus a marked high-rising pitch (written with an acute), with native minimal pairs (hreɲ 'intestine' / hréɲ 'bamboo grub', tal / tál, kaw / káw, ruu / rúu) and native-vs-Tai-loan pairs (kii 'moon' / kíi 'loom', bɔɔ / bɔ́ɔ, kaa / káa); many Tai loans carry the high-rising tone but its pitch does not follow the Lao/Tai Dam tone class of the source (pp. 113-115, fn. 5-6); p. 107: múul 'hill' has 'a marked high tone' vs low unmarked muul in the ethnonym.
